strengths: As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, Affogato addresses an important bottleneck: it scales affordance grounding to 150,104 3D assets, 750,520 language–heatmap pairs, and corresponding 2D supervision, substantially expanding the object and affordance coverage of prior datasets.

The automated Gemma3–Molmo–SAM pipeline is practically attractive and computationally efficient. Multi-view lifting and voting are sensible mechanisms for reducing single-view localization noise, while the shared 2D/3D construction provides useful cross-modal supervision.

The evaluation covers 3D cross-dataset transfer, category-disjoint transfer, 2D zero-shot transfer to AGD20K, full-supervision fine-tuning, and partial observations. In particular, Affogato pretraining yields clear improvements for Espresso-2D on AGD20K, including from KLD/SIM/NSS of 1.034/0.503/1.550 to 0.974/0.519/1.645 after pretraining.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, provides useful implementation and compute details, and openly discusses several pipeline failures, including incorrect queries, SAM edge bias, occluded parts, missing scene context, and ambiguous target objects.
weaknesses: The benchmark ground truth is insufficiently independent of its generation pipeline. Only the 15.4% of sampled test annotations rated “not good” are manually refined; the remaining test labels are largely outputs of the same Molmo/SAM pipeline used to create training supervision. Models may therefore be rewarded for reproducing teacher artifacts. A fully human-annotated test subset, quantitative comparison against human heatmaps, inter-annotator agreement, and precise adjudication procedures are needed. The qualitative comparison in Fig. A2 does not establish annotation accuracy.

The claimed open-vocabulary generalization is not convincingly isolated. Table 3 separates object categories, but the paper does not show that affordance concepts, linguistic templates, or semantic query families are disjoint between training and testing. The fox example is anecdotal. Evaluations on held-out affordances, paraphrases, compositional queries, and genuinely novel interaction concepts are necessary to substantiate the central claim.

The 3D transfer evidence is weaker than the presentation suggests. In Table 2, Affogato-trained models perform substantially worse on LASO than their LASO-trained counterparts—for example, PointRefer aIoU is 0.090 versus 0.192 and Espresso-3D is 0.067 versus 0.178. Emphasizing a smaller normalized “generalization gap” is misleading because it is confounded by differing in-domain baselines and annotation scales; it does not demonstrate improved performance on the existing 3D benchmark.

Important controls are absent. There is no study separating the effects of dataset scale, asset diversity, query diversity, multi-view aggregation, annotation filtering, or the pretrained encoders. Comparisons against training on an equal-sized or quality-filtered subset would be especially important because the audit finds 27.7% of annotations merely “ok” or “not good.”

Several reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent: the public dataset URL is blank; exact prompts, heatmap lifting/voting equations, thresholds, normalization, split construction, category extraction, and deduplication are not specified. SAM variants and citations vary across the main text and appendix. Citation [64] for saliency metrics is an unrelated fetal-ultrasound review, and Fig. A2 incorrectly cites [36] as 3D AffordanceNet rather than [11]. Licensing and redistribution implications for the selected Objaverse assets and generated annotations also require discussion.

Table A2 raises an unresolved validity concern: partial-view evaluation improves markedly over full-view evaluation on nearly every principal metric, despite containing less geometry, while the text describes modest degradation. Because visible-point filtering changes the evaluated support and difficulty, these scores are not directly comparable and do not establish robustness to partial observations.

The model and data remain restricted to isolated synthetic objects and contact-region prediction. Background replacement helps 2D transfer, but there is no evaluation on real 3D scans, clutter, occlusion, embodied interaction success, or pose/force prediction. This limits the strength of the broader real-world and embodied-AI motivation. Overall, the scale and 2D transfer results are promising, but benchmark validity and central open-vocabulary claims need stronger independent evidence, leading to a borderline-reject assessment.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks because Affogato and its generation pipeline are the central contributions. At the reported scale—150,104 objects and 750,520 query–heatmap pairs—the resource could be valuable for affordance research.

The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of existing affordance datasets: restricted object categories, vocabularies, and 3D assets. Connecting 2D and 3D supervision through multi-view rendering is practically useful.

The authors evaluate both 2D and 3D grounding, include cross-dataset experiments, and disclose several pipeline failure modes. Espresso-2D obtains strong AGD20K results, including a measurable improvement from Affogato pretraining.
The presentation is generally understandable, and the supplementary material provides model, training, compute, augmentation, and partial-view details.
weaknesses: The benchmark's ground-truth validity is not established convincingly. Its test annotations originate from the same Gemma3–Molmo–SAM pipeline used to create the training data; only the 15.4% rated "not good" are manually corrected, while "good" and "ok" outputs remain machine-generated. Consequently, evaluation may reward imitation of the annotation models and their biases rather than genuine affordance understanding.

The human study is insufficiently specified for a benchmark paper. It is unclear how the 5,000 pairs were distributed among the 10 experts, whether examples received multiple independent ratings, what agreement was obtained, and how the three criteria map to the single good/ok/not-good judgment. The qualitative comparison with human heatmaps contains only a few selected examples and cannot validate 750K annotations.

The claimed open-vocabulary generalization is weakly tested. Table 3 holds out object categories by separating Daily-Used and Furniture, but does not explicitly hold out affordance concepts, linguistic constructions, or compositional query combinations. Because both splits are labeled by the same foundation-model pipeline, this is primarily cross-category transfer, not compelling evidence of open-vocabulary affordance generalization.

The 3D evidence does not substantiate the broad claim that Affogato improves existing benchmarks. In Table 2, training PointRefer on Affogato yields only 0.090 aIoU on LASO versus 0.192 when trained on LASO; Espresso similarly drops from 0.178 to 0.067. The discussion emphasizes smaller normalized gaps and selected metrics instead of confronting the substantially worse absolute LASO performance.

Important results are internally inconsistent. In Table A2 every method performs markedly better on partial views than on full objects in aIoU, AUC, and SIM, yet the text describes reduced visibility and "modest degradation." This counterintuitive reversal is neither acknowledged nor explained and raises concerns about whether the two settings, labels, or metrics are comparable.

The paper lacks the ablations needed to attribute gains to the proposed dataset or pipeline: there is no dataset-scale curve, no controlled comparison of single-view versus multi-view voting, no alternative annotation-model study, no analysis of automatic-label confidence/filtering, and no variance or significance reporting. On AGD20K, the direct no-pretraining Espresso baseline is already very strong, so architecture and training effects are not adequately separated from the benefit of Affogato.

Core generation and release details are too incomplete for reproducibility. Exact prompts, Molmo parsing and invalid-output handling, SAM-logit processing, 2D-to-3D projection, visibility tests, voting equations, thresholds, normalization, filtering, duplicate handling, and precise train/validation splits are omitted. Licensing and redistribution implications of the selected Objaverse assets are also not discussed.

Several attribution and reporting errors undermine confidence: the saliency metrics are cited to an apparently unrelated fetal-ultrasound review; the supplement cites 3D AffordanceNet as reference [36] although it is [11]; SAM/MobileSAM/SAM2 references are inconsistent; and relative percentage changes are called percentage-point differences. These are individually repairable, but compound the more substantive validation concerns.

The dataset inherits systematic semantic errors, edge-biased SAM masks, occluded-part failures, synthetic isolated-object appearance, and possible source/pretraining overlap. The paper acknowledges some of these issues but does not quantify them across categories or demonstrate that they do not distort model rankings. Given that reliable labels and evaluation are the scientific foundation of a benchmark contribution, these concerns currently favor rejection.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than the default Algorithms/General category. Under that framing, the scale—150,104 3D objects, 750,520 language–heatmap pairs, and corresponding 2D supervision—is substantial and potentially valuable to affordance-grounding research.

The automated Gemma3–Molmo–SAM pipeline is a practical and computationally scalable way to obtain free-form queries and dense multi-view-consistent annotations. The paper also provides useful implementation details, computational costs, failure cases, and a human-refined test set.

The evaluation spans both 3D and 2D grounding, full and partial observations, cross-dataset transfer, non-overlapping object-category splits, zero-shot 2D transfer, and supervised fine-tuning. This breadth is appropriate for demonstrating the utility of a benchmark contribution.

Independent evaluation on AGD20K provides particularly persuasive evidence: Affogato-pretrained Espresso-2D clearly outperforms the tested zero-shot alternatives, and Affogato pretraining consistently improves the same architecture after AGD20K fine-tuning.

The deliberately simple Espresso baselines help isolate the value of the data. Results generally indicate improved transfer and strong performance relative to OpenAD and PointRefer, while the qualitative examples support meaningful part-level localization. The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central annotation-quality evidence is not yet fully convincing. Only 5,000 of 750,520 pairs are evaluated, 15.4% are rated “not good,” and apparently only the test annotations—not the noisy training annotations—are corrected. The paper does not report annotator allocation, inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty, or per-category quality, making it difficult to extrapolate the reported ratings to the full dataset.

Evaluation on the Affogato benchmark is partly circular because its ground truth is produced by the same foundation-model pipeline that supplies training data. Coverage and pairwise heatmap diversity do not directly measure semantic or spatial correctness and can reward diffuse or inconsistent maps. A larger quantitative comparison against independently created human heatmaps would strengthen the dataset’s scientific case.

The claimed open-vocabulary generalization is only partially established. Table 3 guarantees non-overlapping object categories but does not establish that affordance concepts or linguistic formulations are unseen. The fox example is anecdotal; explicit held-out-affordance and compositional language splits would better substantiate the claim.

Reproducibility details for the data engine are incomplete: exact prompts, parsing and rejection rules, projection equations, visibility handling, voting and normalization procedures, SAM-logit processing, and test-refinement protocol are not specified sufficiently. Dataset/code access is also unclear because the abstract says the dataset is public but shows no usable link in the supplied manuscript.

Several experimental details deserve correction or clarification. Cross-dataset relative changes are described as percentage-point differences; some transfer conclusions are sensitive to unequal in-domain baselines; no uncertainty across runs is reported; and the substantially higher partial-view scores than full-view scores contradict the accompanying degradation narrative and likely reflect a change in task difficulty or metric behavior. There are also attribution inconsistencies, including SAM/MobileSAM citations, a duplicated reference, and an apparently unrelated citation for NSS. These issues do not negate the contribution but weaken confidence in the current presentation.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, this work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks: its central contribution is Affogato-750K rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm. The automated pipeline is sensible and scalable: multi-view renderings support VLM-generated queries and points, MobileSAM masks are lifted into 3D, and cross-view voting can suppress view-specific errors. Generating the complete dataset in about 24 hours on eight H100 GPUs demonstrates practical scalability.

The evaluation covers both 3D and 2D transfer. Affogato pretraining improves LASO unseen aIoU for OpenAD, PointRefer, and Espresso-3D, while the 2D results on AGD20K are particularly strong in both zero-shot and fully supervised settings.

The held-out-category filtering experiment is useful evidence that transfer gains are not explained solely by overlap with benchmark test categories. The scale ablation also shows monotonic LASO-unseen improvement from 50K to 750K examples.

The authors provide a corrected, object-disjoint 5K test set, analyze pipeline failures, and acknowledge the synthetic-to-real/background limitation. The paper is generally clear and includes helpful qualitative analyses and implementation details.
weaknesses: The annotation-quality evidence is not yet commensurate with the dataset's scale or the claim that the pipeline is a reliable substitute for manual annotation. Only 84.8% of sampled pairs pass validation, so roughly 15.2% of automatically generated training labels may be defective. The human comparison is qualitative and contains only eight examples; a quantitative comparison against dense human heatmaps is needed.

The human study is underspecified. Each of the 5K pairs appears to be judged by only one annotator because the data are assigned in disjoint subsets; no inter-annotator agreement, acceptance thresholds, annotator qualifications, or compensation is reported. It is also unclear whether coverage and SAM-mask failures in the test pool were corrected, since the construction description mentions removing bad queries and re-annotating incorrect points only.

Reproducibility is presently weak for a dataset paper: Appendix A is titled “Dataset link” but contains no link. Essential generation details are also missing, including exact prompts, parsing rules, the mathematical lifting/voting procedure, split manifests, validation split, and filtering of invalid or unsafe Objaverse assets. Dataset licensing and redistribution constraints are not discussed.

There are material internal inconsistencies. Section 4 says the PartField vision encoder is fine-tuned, whereas Appendix B.2 says the entire vision backbone is frozen. Table A2 reports Affogato aIoU values of 0.237–0.287 without defining its evaluation split or reconciling these values with the percentage-style aIoU in the main tables. The 3D optimizer, learning rate, and several preprocessing details are also absent.

The language sometimes overstates the evidence. Affogato pretraining is not consistently beneficial across metrics: PointRefer degrades on every seen metric, and pretrained Espresso-3D worsens seen and unseen MAE as well as seen AUC. The paper should characterize these tradeoffs rather than claiming consistent improvements.

The 2D comparison does not fully isolate the dataset effect: zero-shot baselines use different pretraining data and potentially very different training budgets. Table 4(b) also does not evaluate Espresso under the weak and one-shot protocols, despite the text claiming the best performance “across all supervision settings.” Multiple seeds, error bars, and significance tests are absent throughout.

The core pipeline is a relatively direct composition of existing foundation models, and the Espresso architectures are intentionally standard. Thus originality and impact depend heavily on releasing a well-documented, legally usable dataset and convincingly establishing label quality; the current missing link and limited quantitative validation leave that case borderline.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General: its main contribution is Affogato-750K, comprising 750K query–heatmap pairs over roughly 150K Objaverse assets, with substantially broader object and affordance coverage than prior 3D affordance datasets.

The automated Gemma3–Molmo–MobileSAM pipeline is simple and scalable, and multi-view lifting/voting is a sensible way to reduce view-specific errors. The authors also quantify failure categories and report an 84.8% success rate on a 5K manually inspected sample.

The transfer results provide evidence that the generated supervision has value. On LASO-unseen, pretraining improves aIoU by 0.9, 4.0, and 2.1 points for OpenAD, PointRefer, and Espresso-3D, respectively. Improvements across multiple architectures are more persuasive than results on the proposed model alone.

The paper includes useful analyses of pretraining scale, held-out-category filtering, cross-domain transfer, resolution, background augmentation, and failure cases. The presentation is generally clear, and the symmetric Espresso baselines offer a practical means of studying both 2D and 3D transfer.
weaknesses: The benchmark ground truth is not validated rigorously enough for a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. Ten annotators inspect disjoint subsets, so no inter-annotator agreement or calibration is measured; rating criteria and acceptance thresholds are underspecified. Failed queries are removed and interaction points are re-annotated, but it is unclear whether erroneous or incomplete SAM heatmaps are independently redrawn. Consequently, the 5K test set may retain the spatial biases of the same automated pipeline being evaluated.

The claimed reliability of the full training corpus is overstated. The audit finds a 15.2% failure rate, yet the manuscript does not describe filtering or correcting the remaining approximately 745K training pairs. The only comparison with genuinely human-authored heatmaps is a small, selected qualitative figure; there is no quantitative comparison on an established manually annotated dataset.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate. Appendix A, titled “Dataset link,” is empty, and no code link is provided. Exact prompts, parsing rules, voting/aggregation equations, thresholds, heatmap normalization, split sizes, sampling procedure for scale ablations, and random-seed variation are missing. There is also a direct contradiction: Section 4 says the pretrained 3D vision and text encoders are fine-tuned, whereas Appendix B.2 says the entire vision backbone is frozen.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 4 reports Espresso only under full supervision, yet the text claims it is best “across all supervision settings”; no Espresso weakly supervised or one-shot results are shown. Likewise, pretraining is not consistently beneficial on LASO: PointRefer loses on all four seen metrics, while Espresso-3D's seen AUC and MAE and unseen MAE worsen. These degradations deserve analysis rather than being downplayed.

The 2D comparisons are not well controlled. Espresso-2D receives 750K task-specific affordance examples, while zero-shot competitors use their respective, often much smaller or differently targeted pretraining sources. This establishes the utility of massive task-specific supervision but does not isolate annotation quality or yield a clean model comparison. Matched-data baselines, comparisons to simpler pseudo-labeling strategies, and compute/data-controlled ablations are needed.

The pipeline itself is an incremental composition of existing models, and key design choices receive only qualitative support. In particular, CoT prompting and smallest-mask selection lack quantitative ablations; multi-view voting is not compared against single-view or alternative fusion schemes; and the coverage/diversity statistics are insufficiently defined. The scale analysis also shows 2D KLD saturating by 400K examples, weakening the broad “at scale” conclusion for that modality.

Dataset governance and scope are underdeveloped. The manuscript does not discuss release licensing and redistribution constraints for web-crawled Objaverse assets and generated annotations, nor model-induced cultural or safety biases in proposed interactions. Evaluation is largely on isolated objects, and the claimed relevance to embodied agents is supported only by a few qualitative robot-scene examples, with no manipulation or action-success evaluation.

strengths: Best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than the default Algorithms/General type: its main value is Affogato-750K and the scalable annotation pipeline, while Espresso serves primarily to validate the data. Under that framing, the scale—750K query-heatmap pairs over roughly 150K objects—and breadth across 2D and 3D affordance grounding constitute a significant contribution.

The automated pipeline is sensible and well motivated: multi-view rendering, language-based interaction-point prediction, segmentation, and 3D voting combine complementary foundation models to produce spatially consistent supervision.

The empirical case is broad. Pretraining is evaluated on LASO and AGD20K, under seen, unseen, zero-shot, and supervised settings, and benefits not only Espresso but also prior architectures such as OpenAD, PointRefer, and AffordanceNet.

The strongest evidence concerns generalization: LASO unseen aIoU improves from 14.6 to 18.6 for PointRefer and from 18.7 to 20.8 for Espresso-3D, while Espresso-2D substantially exceeds the reported zero-shot baselines on both AGD20K splits.

Useful analyses address several plausible confounds, including held-out-category filtering, increasing pretraining-set size, background augmentation, resolution, cross-domain asymmetry, pipeline failure modes, and synthetic-to-real transfer examples.

The paper is clearly organized, visually effective, and unusually transparent about the pipeline's 84.8% validation success rate and its main error sources. A human-verified and corrected 5K test set is an important safeguard.
weaknesses: Training-label quality is insufficiently established for a dataset contribution. The 84.8% success estimate uses disjoint subsets assigned to ten annotators, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported; pass criteria and rating aggregation are also underspecified. The remaining approximately 15% error rate in the automatically generated training data may be consequential.

The human-versus-pipeline comparison is qualitative only. Quantitative agreement on an independently annotated set—broken down by semantic validity, localization accuracy, and coverage—would more convincingly support claims that the automated annotations are reliable substitutes for manual labels.

Some conclusions overstate consistency. In Table 2, pretraining worsens PointRefer on all seen metrics, slightly lowers Espresso-3D seen AUC, and substantially worsens Espresso-3D MAE in both seen and unseen settings. The evidence supports improved unseen aIoU/SIM more strongly than uniformly improved grounding.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate: the supplementary 'Dataset link' section is empty, no code or download location is supplied, and release format, filtering details, prompts, aggregation equations, splits, and licensing conditions for the Objaverse-derived data are not fully documented.

There is a methodological inconsistency: Section 4 states that Espresso-3D fine-tunes both the PartField vision encoder and text encoder, whereas the supplement says the entire vision backbone is frozen. This affects reproducibility and interpretation of the gains.

The open-vocabulary diversity claims rely on Gemma-predicted category and affordance names with frequency thresholds, but the normalization, synonym handling, and accuracy of the reported >450 object and >350 affordance counts are unclear. The data are also highly imbalanced toward Daily-Used objects.

Evidence for real-world embodied applicability remains preliminary: Figure 7 contains only four qualitative robot-scene examples, with no quantitative evaluation or downstream manipulation experiment. The limitations discussion should also address inherited foundation-model biases and licensing/privacy risks from web-crawled Objaverse assets.
